title: Concurrent Market Data Pipeline
context:
Market-data handlers are the canonical high-performance concurrency workload: many producers streaming ticks, a bounded hand-off, and consumers aggregating per-symbol statistics in real time. Get the design wrong and you get either a bottleneck (one global lock) or a race (two consumers double-counting a tick). Both failure modes are common in production and in interviews, where 'build a concurrent pipeline and measure it' is a standard senior-level exercise.

The progression in this project is deliberate: build the correct mutex+condvar version first, prove its numbers, then replace the queue with a lock-free implementation and measure the difference. The engineering lesson — correct before fast, and measure claims — is the deliverable as much as the code.
problem:
Build a concurrent tick-processing pipeline in C++17:

- **Producers**: P threads simulate ticks (geometric-Brownian-motion prices per symbol from a fixed seed) and push into a bounded queue.
- **Queue**: two implementations behind one interface — (a) mutex + condition-variable bounded queue (starter provided), (b) a lock-free bounded ring using atomics — switchable by config.
- **Consumers**: C threads pop ticks and aggregate per-symbol statistics: count, mean, population stddev (Welford), min, max. Aggregation must be race-free (shard symbols across consumers, or merge per-consumer partials at the end — your choice, documented).
- **Correctness**: for a fixed seed and workload, the concurrent run's per-symbol stats must exactly match a single-threaded reference; total consumed ticks == total produced (no lost or duplicated ticks); the suite runs cleanly under ThreadSanitizer.
- **Shutdown**: close semantics drain the queue; all consumers exit; all threads join; no deadlock under stress.
- **Measurements**: end-to-end throughput (ticks/sec) and queue latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99/max in ns, measured enqueue-to-dequeue) across a small matrix of (P, C, capacity) — results table in the docs, with commentary on where the bottleneck moves.
requirements: One queue interface with both implementations; the mutex+condvar starter is provided and must pass the correctness suite before the lock-free variant is attempted.

The lock-free variant uses C++11 atomics with explicit memory-order reasoning documented (release/acquire pairs and why); false-sharing guards (cache-line padding) on hot per-thread counters are required and their effect measured.
No lost or duplicated ticks under any (P, C, capacity) tested; the count invariant is asserted in every run, including abrupt producer completion.
Per-symbol aggregation matches the serial reference exactly on fixed seeds for both queue implementations.
Graceful shutdown: producers finish, queue closed, consumers drain and exit, all threads joined within a timeout; stress test with unbalanced producer speeds.

Latency percentiles computed from per-tick enqueue/dequeue timestamps collected in a preallocated results buffer (no allocation in the measurement path); the percentile code itself is unit-tested on a known sample.

Benchmark matrix (e.g. P in {1, 2, 4}, C in {1, 2, 4}, capacity in {1024, 16384}) reported for both queue implementations with a written comparison; the fastest configuration's bottleneck identified by profiling or reasoning.

designGuidance.code:
P producers ──► [ bounded queue ] ──► C consumers ──► per-symbol aggregates
  (GBM simulators)   (mutex or lock-free)   (shard by symbol hash,
                                             or merge partials at end)

designGuidance.md: Two aggregation designs are acceptable. **Sharding**: consumer k owns symbols where hash(symbol) mod C == k — no shared aggregation state at all, at the cost of load imbalance when symbols are hot. **Partials**: every consumer aggregates everything it sees; at shutdown the C partial Welford accumulators merge in O(C * symbols). Welford state merges exactly (n, mean and M2 combine analytically) — do the derivation in a comment.

designGuidance.title: False sharing eats your throughput
designGuidance.md: If two threads write to counters that share a 64-byte cache line, the line ping-pongs and your 'lock-free' queue measures slower than the mutex one. Pad hot per-thread counters (`alignas(64)`) and measure before/after — the delta is the whole lesson.

designGuidance.title: Queue latency measurement protocol
items: Producer stamps each tick with steady_clock::now() at enqueue (timestamps live in the Tick struct — no side allocations).
Consumer stamps dequeue and appends (dequeue - enqueue) into a preallocated vector or fixed ring sized to the workload.
After drain, sort the deltas once and read off p50/p95/p99/max; report the mean too.
Separate latency runs from throughput runs — computing percentiles in the hot loop changes the very latency you measure (batching effects), so never do both in one pass.

designGuidance.title: TSan is part of the spec
designGuidance.md: A concurrency project that has not run under ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) is unverified. Make the TSan run a script, record it in the README, and treat any reported race — even one you 'know' is benign — as a defect to explain or fix.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Concurrency correctness: count invariants, exact match vs serial reference, TSan-clean
Lock-free implementation: sound memory ordering, false-sharing handling, documented reasoning
Measurement quality: latency percentile protocol, throughput matrix, honest comparison
Shutdown semantics and stress robustness (unbalanced producers, drain, joins)

documentationRequirements: README.md: topology diagram, queue implementations and the switch, build/run including the TSan script.
Memory-ordering section: every atomic operation in the lock-free queue annotated with its ordering and why it suffices.
RESULTS.md: throughput/latency tables over the (P, C, capacity) matrix for both queues, plus interpretation.
Shutdown-semantics spec: the close/drain/join contract that tests rely on.
extensionChallenges: Implement an MPSC lock-free queue (Vyukov-style) and compare against your SPSC design under asymmetric producer loads.
Add adaptive batching: consumers pop up to k ticks at once; measure the throughput/latency trade-off curve.
Pin threads to cores (pthread_setaffinity_np) and quantify the jitter reduction in p99 latency.
